Pre-Incorporation & Know-Your-Customer

UBO Ultimate Beneficial Owner Screening Rules Official Registry Only

>=25% ownership / control

Applicable AML statute: Ley 10/2010, de 28 de abril, de prevención del blanqueo de capitales y de la financiación del terrorismo, as amended by Ley 11/2021, de 9 de julio; Real Decreto 304/2014, de 5 de mayo, approving the Reglamento de la Ley 10/2010; Ley 6/2023, de 17 de marzo, de los Mercados de Valores y de los Servicios de Inversión; Real Decreto-ley 7/2021, de 27 de abril, transposing the Fifth and Sixth Anti-Money Laundering Directives; Real Decreto 95/2024, de 23 de enero, regulating the Single Register of Ultimate Beneficial Owners (Registro Único de Titularidades Reales); Orden JUS/319/2018 establishing the technical specifications for the Registro Central de Titularidades Reales.
Registered Agent & Physical Address Licensed Agent Required

A virtual office is accepted only as an ancillary administrative address where the SL maintains a genuine physical registered office in Spain at which the legal address (domicilio social) is fixed, where the deed and the Registro Mercantil entry state a valid street address, and where correspondence can be physically received by an appointed person with authority to represent the company. It is not permissible as a substitute for the statutory registered office for purposes of article 9 of the Spanish Capital Companies Law (Real Decreto Legislativo 1/2010), which requires the registered office to be located in Spanish territory, to coincide with the actual place of effective management and administration, or with the place where the center of actual business activity is located unless the articles of association provide otherwise. For a commercial litigation chamber with a cross-border arbitration and asset tracing practice, the legal framework under the Ley 2/2007 (Sociedades Profesionales), when applicable, and the obligations imposed by the Spanish Lawyers' Code (Estatuto General de la Abogacía Española, approved by Royal Decree 135/2021) require a physical office with adequate client confidentiality, professional record-keeping, evidence-retention capacity, and a secure trust account (IOLTA) arrangement. Therefore the use of an exclusive virtual office for the registered address is not permitted; a managed office or a serviced office with a permanent Spanish presence, adequate file storage and professional facilities may be used.

✓ Partner licensed company-secretary channels provide local registered address and government mail forwarding.

Stage 03

Tax Identity & Indirect Tax

Tax authority e-portal, entity tax classification elections, VAT thresholds, and 0% export documentation chain.

Tax ID Application Infrastructure

Competent tax authority

Agencia Estatal de Administración Tributaria (AEAT), administered through the AEAT Electronic Headquarters (Sede electrónica): https://sede.agenciatributaria.gob.es. The competent regional tax authorities of the Autonomous Communities may administer certain regional taxes, but national corporate income tax, VAT, customs, and NIF administration are generally handled by the AEAT.

E-government filing portal

A Spanish Sociedad de Responsabilidad Limitada must obtain a Número de Identificación Fiscal (NIF) from the AEAT. The incorporation process generally comprises: (1) obtain the corporate name certificate from the Central Mercantile Registry; (2) execute the incorporation deed before a Spanish notary; (3) submit Modelo 036 to the AEAT for a provisional NIF, normally with the deed or incorporation documents, shareholder and director identification, registered office, activity classification, and representation evidence; (4) register the company with the competent Mercantile Registry; (5) submit the registered deed and final corporate documentation to the AEAT to obtain or confirm the definitive NIF; and (6) update Modelo 036 for commencement of activities, VAT obligations, intra-Community transactions, withholding obligations, and other applicable census registrations. The Spanish NIF is generally also the VAT identification number, expressed for intra-Community purposes as ES plus the NIF. Registration in the Registro de Operadores Intracomunitarios (ROI) and inclusion in the VIES system must be requested through Modelo 036 before carrying out qualifying intra-Community transactions. Foreign shareholders, directors, and foreign entities generally require an applicable Spanish NIF or NIE and must provide notarised, apostilled or legalised, and officially translated documents where required. A foreign entity conducting taxable business in Spain without a Spanish subsidiary may obtain a Spanish NIF and, where applicable, register for VAT through Modelo 036; a Spanish tax representative may be required in specified non-EU or non-established situations.

Tax ID type & application path: Entity_Level_Taxation — A Spanish Sociedad de Responsabilidad Limitada must obtain a Número de Identificación Fiscal (NIF) from the AEAT. The incorporation process generally comprises: (1) obtain the corporate name certificate from the Central Mercantile Registry; (2) execute the incorporation deed before a Spanish notary; (3) submit Modelo 036 to the AEAT for a provisional NIF, normally with the deed or incorporation documents, shareholder and director identification, registered office, activity classification, and representation evidence; (4) register the company with the competent Mercantile Registry; (5) submit the registered deed and final corporate documentation to the AEAT to obtain or confirm the definitive NIF; and (6) update Modelo 036 for commencement of activities, VAT obligations, intra-Community transactions, withholding obligations, and other applicable census registrations. The Spanish NIF is generally also the VAT identification number, expressed for intra-Community purposes as ES plus the NIF. Registration in the Registro de Operadores Intracomunitarios (ROI) and inclusion in the VIES system must be requested through Modelo 036 before carrying out qualifying intra-Community transactions. Foreign shareholders, directors, and foreign entities generally require an applicable Spanish NIF or NIE and must provide notarised, apostilled or legalised, and officially translated documents where required. A foreign entity conducting taxable business in Spain without a Spanish subsidiary may obtain a Spanish NIF and, where applicable, register for VAT through Modelo 036; a Spanish tax representative may be required in specified non-EU or non-established situations.

Default Tax Classification & Elections

Default tax classification

Entity_Level_Taxation

Available election forms

Spain does not operate a general United States-style check-the-box election for an Sociedad de Responsabilidad Limitada. The SL is ordinarily subject to Spanish corporate income tax as a separate legal person. Available elective or special mechanisms may include the tax consolidation regime for qualifying corporate groups, the special regime for qualifying newly created entities, the regime for small entities where statutory conditions are met, the restructuring regime for qualifying mergers, demergers, contributions, and exchanges, and other sector-specific or territorial regimes. Tax consolidation and other special regimes require statutory eligibility and timely formal election or notification. Hybrid mismatch rules under the Anti-Tax Avoidance Directive framework may deny deductions, include amounts in taxable income, or restrict relief; they are not a general entity-classification election.

VAT / GST & 0% Export Zero-Rating

Standard VAT / GST rate

21%

Mandatory registration threshold (Nexus)

No general economic turnover threshold applies for Spanish VAT registration. A person or entity carrying out an economic activity independently in Spain is generally required to register from commencement or from the point at which taxable activity begins, regardless of turnover. The annual turnover threshold historically relevant to certain simplified or special regimes does not create a general exemption from ordinary VAT registration for an SL.

Export 0% zero-rating conditions

Exports of goods from the Spanish VAT territory to destinations outside the European Union may qualify for VAT exemption with the right to deduct input VAT where the goods leave the EU and the supplier can substantiate the export. Intra-Community supplies of goods may qualify for exemption with the right to deduct input VAT where the purchaser is identified for VAT in another EU Member State, the goods are transported from Spain to that Member State, and the supplier satisfies the reporting and evidentiary requirements, including the purchaser's valid VAT number and the applicable recapitulative statement requirements. Cross-border services must be analysed separately: qualifying B2B services are generally outside the scope of Spanish VAT under the place-of-supply rules when supplied to a business established outside Spain, rather than being technically zero-rated exports. Specific exceptions apply, including services connected with Spanish immovable property, admission to events, passenger transport, certain restaurant and catering services, short-term means of transport hire, and other statutory categories. Export or exemption claims require consistent invoices, transport evidence, customs or intra-Community reporting evidence, customer status verification, and accounting records.

  • Electronic Customs Export Declaration or equivalent customs export record, including the export accompanying document and the customs exit confirmation or equivalent electronic proof of exit
  • Commercial invoice identifying the supplier, customer, goods, value, delivery terms, and applicable VAT exemption reference
  • Transport documentation, such as bill of lading, airway bill, CMR consignment note, courier record, or equivalent evidence showing movement from Spain or the EU to the destination outside the EU
  • Packing list and shipping or delivery records where relevant to identify the exported goods
  • Proof of payment or commercial settlement and accounting records linking the transaction to the export
  • For intra-Community supplies, the customer's valid EU VAT identification number, transport evidence, and correctly filed recapitulative statement (Modelo 349)
  • Import or destination-country customs evidence where reasonably available
  • An inward remittance certificate is not a universal Spanish legal prerequisite for applying the export exemption; bank payment records may nevertheless support transaction and audit substantiation

Spanish VAT invoices must comply with the electronic invoicing and invoice-content rules under the Spanish invoicing regulations. Electronic invoices require authenticity of origin, integrity of content, legibility, recipient acceptance where applicable, and secure retention; qualified electronic signatures, approved electronic exchange systems, or reliable audit controls may be used. The Immediate Supply of Information system (Suministro Inmediato de Información, SII) requires qualifying taxpayers, including taxpayers registered in the monthly VAT refund regime, entities applying the VAT group regime, and businesses exceeding the statutory large-enterprise turnover threshold, to transmit prescribed invoice-register data electronically to the AEAT, generally within the applicable four- or eight-business-day periods. SII is not a universal real-time clearance mandate for every SL. Spain has legislated broader B2B electronic-invoicing obligations under Law 18/2022, but their operational application depends on implementing regulations and legally effective commencement dates. Accordingly, an SL must monitor the final technical and transitional rules before treating universal B2B real-time clearance, an AEAT pre-clearance requirement, or mandatory digital stamping as currently applicable.

Spain has no general statutory requirement that export proceeds be repatriated within 180 days as a condition of Spanish VAT exemption. The exporter must retain evidence supporting the goods' exit from the EU, the applicable customer and transport conditions, and the accounting treatment for the statutory record-retention period. If the exemption is incorrectly claimed, the AEAT may assess unpaid VAT, late-payment interest, and applicable penalties, and may deny or reverse input-VAT deductions or refund claims. Serious or deliberate infringement may attract proportional penalties based on the unpaid or improperly refunded tax, subject to the General Tax Law, with aggravation for concealment, fraudulent means, repeated non-compliance, or use of false or inauthentic documentation. Incorrect invoices may require corrective invoices and VAT adjustments. False customs declarations may also trigger customs debt, customs penalties, seizure or forfeiture measures, and potentially criminal liability in cases involving tax fraud or smuggling. VAT refund claims remain subject to audit, documentary verification, limitation periods, and clawback of amounts improperly refunded.

Stage 04

Banking & Treasury Architecture

Central-bank FX diagnosis, tier-1 local banks vs offshore digital EMI matrix, and KYC rejection defense guide.

Foreign Exchange Regime & Central Bank Policy

Current-account convertibility

Spain uses the euro and applies EU Treaty principles on free movement of capital. Current-account payments, including imports, exports, professional fees, dividends, interest, royalties, and ordinary service payments, are generally freely transferable without exchange-control approval. Capital-account transactions are also generally liberalized, but foreign investment reporting, beneficial ownership transparency, anti-money laundering controls, sanctions screening, and potential prior authorization may apply. Investments by non-EU or non-EEA persons in regulated or strategically sensitive sectors may be subject to Spain's foreign direct investment screening regime under Law 19/2003 and Royal Decree 571/2023. Dividend and profit remittances require distributable profits, approved financial statements, corporate-law compliance, withholding-tax analysis, and evidence of the underlying transaction. Payments from client or litigation trust funds must be segregated, supported by client instructions or court documentation, and must not be treated as corporate distributable cash.

Export proceeds surrender rules

Spain has no general statutory requirement to surrender export proceeds to a Spanish bank and no mandatory conversion ratio for export receipts. Exporters may retain foreign-currency proceeds in foreign or Spanish accounts, subject to ordinary banking, accounting, tax, sanctions, and anti-money laundering controls. Banks may request commercial invoices, transport documents, customs evidence, contracts, and proof of beneficial ownership. Cross-border transfers may be included in statistical or balance-of-payments reporting performed by financial institutions or required under applicable reporting rules. Any conversion should be performed through an authorized credit institution or other duly authorized payment or investment-services provider.

Central bank supervision: Banco de España, operating within the Eurosystem under the European Central Bank framework. Foreign investment and certain external economic transaction reporting is administered by the Directorate-General for International Trade and Investments of the Spanish Ministry of Economy, Commerce and Business.

Offshore Digital Bank / EMI Whitelist

Cross-border EMI / Fintech rails Fit: High

Medium for ordinary corporate operating payments and foreign-exchange execution; Low to Medium for client-money or litigation-trust functions. An electronic money institution or payment institution authorized in the EEA may provide cross-border services into Spain through passporting and applicable notification procedures. A non-EEA fintech does not obtain equivalent access merely by operating offshore and may require a Spanish or EEA authorization, branch, agent, or regulated banking partner. EMIs safeguard funds but do not provide bank deposits, deposit-guarantee protection, or unrestricted escrow functionality. Client funds for legal services should be maintained only in an arrangement accepted by the relevant Spanish Bar rules, professional regulations, bank, and applicable anti-money laundering controls. Offshore digital EMIs may impose country, sector, source-of-funds, litigation, and high-risk-client restrictions.

Core KYC Rejection Triggers & Defense Dossier

Unclear ownership, nominee shareholders, unexplained control rights, or inability to identify the ultimate beneficial owner.

Root cause: Unclear ownership, nominee shareholders, unexplained control rights, or inability to identify the ultimate beneficial owner.

Defense evidence: Current Spanish commercial registry extract; notarized articles of association; shareholder register; ownership chart to natural persons; passport and address evidence for each beneficial owner, director, and signatory; UBO declaration; corporate resolutions; and confirmation of voting and control rights.
Foreign shareholders, directors, or beneficial owners lacking Spanish tax identification numbers or presenting inconsistent names and addresses across documents.

Root cause: Foreign shareholders, directors, or beneficial owners lacking Spanish tax identification numbers or presenting inconsistent names and addresses across documents.

Defense evidence: NIE or NIF documentation where required; certified passports; recent utility or bank statements; apostilled corporate documents; sworn Spanish translations where requested; tax-residency certificates; and a reconciliation memorandum explaining all name, address, and registration-number discrepancies.
Law-firm or commercial-litigation activity involving client funds, court awards, asset tracing, third-party settlements, or a proposed IOLTA-style account.

Root cause: Law-firm or commercial-litigation activity involving client funds, court awards, asset tracing, third-party settlements, or a proposed IOLTA-style account.

Defense evidence: Professional-company and Bar-registration evidence; engagement-letter template; client-money policy; account segregation policy; three-way reconciliation procedure; authorized signatory matrix; source-and-purpose-of-funds controls; client identification and sanctions procedures; court orders or settlement agreements where applicable; and written confirmation that client funds will not be commingled with corporate operating funds.
High-volume international wires, payments involving Latin America, third-party payors, cash-intensive clients, or transfers unrelated to the stated litigation and arbitration business.

Root cause: High-volume international wires, payments involving Latin America, third-party payors, cash-intensive clients, or transfers unrelated to the stated litigation and arbitration business.

Defense evidence: Annual transaction forecast by corridor and currency; client and matter taxonomy; representative engagement letters; invoices; court or arbitration documentation; counterparties' ownership information; source-of-funds and source-of-wealth files; expected payment-purpose schedule; sanctions-screening records; and documented escalation procedures.
Use of cryptocurrency, virtual-asset platforms, unregulated payment intermediaries, privacy-enhancing tools, or opaque layered transfers.

Root cause: Use of cryptocurrency, virtual-asset platforms, unregulated payment intermediaries, privacy-enhancing tools, or opaque layered transfers.

Defense evidence: Board-approved prohibition or restricted-use policy; wallet ownership evidence; exchange regulatory status; blockchain transaction reports; independent source-of-funds analysis; transaction rationale; tax records; and written bank pre-clearance before any related transfer.
Large capital injection, shareholder loan, dividend, or intercompany transfer with no demonstrable economic purpose or inadequate accounting support.

Root cause: Large capital injection, shareholder loan, dividend, or intercompany transfer with no demonstrable economic purpose or inadequate accounting support.

Defense evidence: Shareholder or board resolutions; capital-increase deed where applicable; shareholder-loan agreement; transfer-pricing support; financial statements; solvency analysis; beneficial-owner confirmation; proof of originating account; foreign-investment reporting evidence where applicable; and accounting entries matching the bank narrative.
Potential sanctions, politically exposed person status, adverse media, corruption exposure, or involvement in jurisdictions subject to enhanced monitoring.

Root cause: Potential sanctions, politically exposed person status, adverse media, corruption exposure, or involvement in jurisdictions subject to enhanced monitoring.

Defense evidence: Enhanced due-diligence report; independent identity and ownership verification; PEP declarations; sanctions-screening results; adverse-media resolution file; legal opinion on permissibility; transaction-level approvals; and senior-management sign-off.
Inability to demonstrate a genuine Spanish operating nexus, especially where the company is newly incorporated or managed primarily from abroad.

Root cause: Inability to demonstrate a genuine Spanish operating nexus, especially where the company is newly incorporated or managed primarily from abroad.

Defense evidence: Lease or registered-office evidence; employment and adviser agreements; Spanish tax registrations; Bar or professional registration; business plan; client and supplier contracts; website and professional profiles; expected payroll and tax flows; and evidence of local management and record retention.

Cross-Border Clearing Corridors & Settlement Fit

Route equity through a Spanish credit institution into the company's designated capital account before execution of the notarial incorporation or capital-increase documentation, or into the operating account after registration where permitted. Use the shareholder's own bank account and an exact payment narrative identifying the company, shareholder, transaction type, and currency. Maintain the bank certificate or transfer confirmation, notarial deed, corporate resolution, beneficial-owner evidence, source-of-funds documentation, and accounting entry. For shareholder loans, use a written agreement stating principal, maturity, interest, repayment, subordination if applicable, and transfer-pricing basis. Assess foreign-investment reporting under Royal Decree 571/2023, sectoral screening under Law 19/2003, tax withholding, transfer-pricing, and related-party reporting. Do not route capital through client, escrow, personal, or unrelated third-party accounts. Confirm with the receiving bank whether a payment-purpose code, regulatory declaration, or supporting document is required; Spain generally does not impose a universal central-bank purpose-code regime for ordinary corporate capital transfers.Use SEPA Credit Transfer for euro payments within the SEPA area and SWIFT customer credit transfer, commonly MT103 or its ISO 20022 equivalent, for non-SEPA or non-euro corridors. Match every payment to an invoice, engagement letter, purchase order, settlement agreement, court order, tax document, or other underlying record. For litigation and arbitration matters, distinguish operating expenses, client-money disbursements, settlement payments, court fees, expert fees, and distributions to the client. Use a commercial documentary letter of credit, including an irrevocable letter of credit confirmed where justified, for genuine trade transactions involving documentary performance and bank-controlled payment conditions; it is generally unsuitable for ordinary legal fees or unverified client settlements. Apply dual approval, sanctions screening, beneficiary-account verification, maker-checker controls, payment limits, callback verification for account changes, and three-way reconciliation. Retain SWIFT confirmations, invoices, customs or transport documents where relevant, withholding-tax analysis, and evidence of client authorization for fiduciary payments.Deliverable foreign-exchange forwards with an authorized EU bank or investment firm, documented under appropriate master terms and subject to suitability, appropriateness, collateral, reporting, and EMIR requirements where applicable.Non-deliverable forwards for currencies with restricted convertibility, subject to counterparty authorization, jurisdictional legality, bank risk limits, valuation controls, and prohibition on using the instrument for speculative activity unrelated to documented exposure.Currency swaps and cross-currency swaps for recurring or material currency exposures, subject to ISDA or equivalent documentation, EMIR classification and reporting, collateral and margin requirements where applicable, and board-approved counterparty limits.FX options or collars for documented receivable, payable, settlement, or dividend exposures, subject to MiFID II classification, product-governance, valuation, disclosure, and risk-management requirements.Spot foreign-exchange conversions through authorized credit institutions or regulated payment providers for ordinary settlement needs; maintain a documented exposure register and prohibit unapproved directional trading.Hedging policy requirements: define eligible exposures, hedge ratios, tenor limits, approved counterparties, collateral authority, accounting treatment, independent valuation, termination rights, stress testing, and quarterly board or treasury-committee reporting.

E-commerce / gateway settlement fit: Medium for ordinary corporate operating payments and foreign-exchange execution; Low to Medium for client-money or litigation-trust functions. An electronic money institution or payment institution authorized in the EEA may provide cross-border services into Spain through passporting and applicable notification procedures. A non-EEA fintech does not obtain equivalent access merely by operating offshore and may require a Spanish or EEA authorization, branch, agent, or regulated banking partner. EMIs safeguard funds but do not provide bank deposits, deposit-guarantee protection, or unrestricted escrow functionality. Client funds for legal services should be maintained only in an arrangement accepted by the relevant Spanish Bar rules, professional regulations, bank, and applicable anti-money laundering controls. Offshore digital EMIs may impose country, sector, source-of-funds, litigation, and high-risk-client restrictions.

Stage 06

Corporate Tax & Transfer Pricing

Corporate income tax (CIT), box-by-box return breakdown, dividend WHT, and director personal liability.

Statutory corporate income tax (CIT)

25%

Dividend withholding tax (WHT)

19% statutory IRNR withholding on gross Spanish-source dividends and participation profits paid to non-resident shareholders. The EU Parent-Subsidiary Directive may reduce the rate to 0% where the EU parent directly holds at least 5% of the SL's capital for at least 12 months and holds real beneficial-ownership substance.

Mandatory Return Breakdown

Deadline: · Frequency:

Modelo 200 must be filed within 25 calendar days following the six-month anniversary of the fiscal year end. For calendar-year taxpayers this means July 1 to July 25 of the following year.

Box-by-Box Return Breakdown (non-resident focus)

BoxField Non-resident guidanceTax-evasion pitfall
Box 001 - NIF Taxpayer identification number of the Spanish SL. Enter the NIF assigned by AEAT to the Spanish permanent establishment or branch; a foreign registration number is not acceptable. Late filing without AEAT request triggers surcharges under LGT Article 27: 5% within 3 months, 10% within 6 months, 15% within 12 months, and 20% after 12 months, plus late-payment interest. A formal administrative inspection assessment can produce penalties from 50% to 150% of the undeclared tax. Criminal liability arises under Penal Code Article 305 when the defrauded amount exceeds EUR 120,000 per tax period.
Box 002 - Tax Period Opening and closing dates of the fiscal year in DD/MM/YYYY format. The fiscal period must match the branch accounts kept in Spain and may not exceed 12 months without prior AEAT approval. Late filing without AEAT request triggers surcharges under LGT Article 27: 5% within 3 months, 10% within 6 months, 15% within 12 months, and 20% after 12 months, plus late-payment interest. A formal administrative inspection assessment can produce penalties from 50% to 150% of the undeclared tax. Criminal liability arises under Penal Code Article 305 when the defrauded amount exceeds EUR 120,000 per tax period.
Box 009 - Declaration Type Selection of ordinary, limited, or consolidated scheme. A Spanish PE or branch always files the ordinary declaration; simplified filing is not available to foreign-owned branches. Late filing without AEAT request triggers surcharges under LGT Article 27: 5% within 3 months, 10% within 6 months, 15% within 12 months, and 20% after 12 months, plus late-payment interest. A formal administrative inspection assessment can produce penalties from 50% to 150% of the undeclared tax. Criminal liability arises under Penal Code Article 305 when the defrauded amount exceeds EUR 120,000 per tax period.
Box 102 - Book Profit or Loss Pre-tax accounting result per statutory annual accounts prepared under Spanish GAAP. Use the branch's standalone Spanish GAAP accounts; eliminate intercompany transactions lacking substance and economic purpose. Late filing without AEAT request triggers surcharges under LGT Article 27: 5% within 3 months, 10% within 6 months, 15% within 12 months, and 20% after 12 months, plus late-payment interest. A formal administrative inspection assessment can produce penalties from 50% to 150% of the undeclared tax. Criminal liability arises under Penal Code Article 305 when the defrauded amount exceeds EUR 120,000 per tax period.
Box 103 - Tax Adjustments Permanent and temporary adjustments converting book profit into taxable base. Add non-deductible expenses, disallow invoices from shell intermediaries, and reflect transfer pricing corrections for cross-border services. Late filing without AEAT request triggers surcharges under LGT Article 27: 5% within 3 months, 10% within 6 months, 15% within 12 months, and 20% after 12 months, plus late-payment interest. A formal administrative inspection assessment can produce penalties from 50% to 150% of the undeclared tax. Criminal liability arises under Penal Code Article 305 when the defrauded amount exceeds EUR 120,000 per tax period.
Box 114 - Transfer Pricing Documentation Flag Declaration that contemporaneous TP documentation has been prepared and retained. Confirm whether Local File/Master File thresholds are met for the Spanish branch or parent group. Late filing without AEAT request triggers surcharges under LGT Article 27: 5% within 3 months, 10% within 6 months, 15% within 12 months, and 20% after 12 months, plus late-payment interest. A formal administrative inspection assessment can produce penalties from 50% to 150% of the undeclared tax. Criminal liability arises under Penal Code Article 305 when the defrauded amount exceeds EUR 120,000 per tax period.
Box 200 - Tax Payable or Refund Application of statutory rates, deductions, prepayments, and final tax result. Apply the 25% general rate unless a reduced new-entity 15% rate or treaty provision is substantiated in the return. Late filing without AEAT request triggers surcharges under LGT Article 27: 5% within 3 months, 10% within 6 months, 15% within 12 months, and 20% after 12 months, plus late-payment interest. A formal administrative inspection assessment can produce penalties from 50% to 150% of the undeclared tax. Criminal liability arises under Penal Code Article 305 when the defrauded amount exceeds EUR 120,000 per tax period.

Transfer Pricing & Economic Substance

Master / Local File threshold: EUR 10,000,000.00 prior-year net turnover triggers mandatory preparation and retention of a Spanish Local File. A Master File is required when the consolidated group's total net revenue exceeds EUR 75,000,000.00. For litigation and asset-tracing chambers with related-party transactions in excess of EUR 250,000.00 in a year, contemporaneous TP documentation is prudent even where the formal threshold is not met.

Economic substance scope: Spain is a unitary national jurisdiction and does not implement Economic Substance Regulations as a separate statute comparable to UAE ESR. However, the Spanish anti-abuse doctrine, LIS Article 15 substantial-purpose provisions, Article 18 related-party rules, and ATAD transposition require the Spanish SL to demonstrate real personnel, offices, management, board proceedings, and substantive commercial activity. In cross-border commercial litigation and asset tracing, the Spanish entity must evidence autonomous case management and client files; otherwise treaty benefits, PE attribution, and EU directive exemptions will be denied.

Fatal Compliance Red Lines & Director Liability

Tax Evasion and Fraudulent CIT Filing

Statutory sanction: LGT penalty of 50% to 150% of the tax would have been paid; plus late-payment interest and loss of EU subsidies. Criminal conviction under Penal Code Article 305 for tax fraud exceeding EUR 120,000 in a single period carries imprisonment of two to six years, a fine up to six times the defrauded amount, and confiscation of profits.

Director personal liability: Directors who directed, approved, or knowingly tolerated the false return are jointly and severally liable for the entire tax debt. Criminal courts may impose travel bans, embargo of personal and corporate assets, disqualification from managing entities, and immediate imprisonment following final conviction.
Shell Company / Conduit Recharacterization

Statutory sanction: AEAT may recharacterize the transaction under the Spanish GAAR, ignore the SL's separate legal personality, disallow related-party expenses as non-deductible, reclassify fee flows as direct distributions subject to 19% withholding or royalties subject to 24% withholding, and assess penalties of 50% to 150% of the understated tax.

Director personal liability: Veil piercing under Spanish company law applies where the SL is a fiction or facade. Directors and beneficial owners become directly liable for corporate tax debts, loss of distribution rights, restitution to clients in civil insolvency, professional disqualification, and potential travel restrictions during cross-border enforcement.
AML / Money Laundering Through Trust or IOLTA Accounts

Statutory sanction: Law 10/2010 AML administrative penalties for very serious infringements range from EUR 3,000,000 to EUR 100,000,000, or twice the benefit obtained; the listed entity is subject to public naming, loss of statutory license, and forced AML compliance. Money laundering under Penal Code Articles 301-304 carries imprisonment of three to six years, daily fines, and seizure of the trust assets.

Director personal liability: Directors and compliance officers are personally criminally liable where they knowingly process illicit funds or deliberately omit AML systems. Courts may impose frozen account orders, asset seizures, travel bans pending investigation, disqualification from legal practice, and civilian restitution orders against director estates.
Unauthorized Cross-Border Legal Practice and Licensing Violation

Statutory sanction: Bar Council enforcement can impose administrative fines usually ranging from EUR 30,000 to EUR 300,000 per retention, issue a cessation order, and refer the matter for criminal prosecution under Penal Code Article 403 for carrying out a licensed profession without authorization; repeated conduct carries imprisonment up to two years.

Director personal liability: Directors cannot shield behind the SL where they control actual litigation strategy and asset tracing. They are personally liable for client restitution, may be barred from professional registers, disqualified from managing law firms, subjected to travel bans where flight risk is shown, and, on repeated violation, sentenced to imprisonment.
